sources.title: Offline and Falling Behind: Barriers to Internet Adoption
key_facts: As of 2013, the worldwide Internet user population was approximately 2.7 billion people, meaning more than 60 percent of the global population was offline.
Approximately 4.4 billion individuals were offline at the time of the report.
About 75 percent of the offline population (approximately 3.4 billion people) was concentrated in just 20 countries.
Between 1.1 billion and 2.8 billion individuals could not get online via mobile network because they did not live within sufficient mobile network coverage.
Approximately 64 percent of offline individuals lived in rural areas, compared to 24 percent of Internet users who were considered rural.
As much as 50 percent of offline individuals had an income below the average of their respective country's poverty line and median income.
Approximately 28 percent of the offline population was illiterate, while close to 100 percent of the online population could read and write.
An estimated 920 million of the 3.4 billion offline individuals concentrated in 20 countries were illiterate.
52 percent of the offline population was female, while women made up 42 percent of the online population.
18 percent of non-Internet users were seniors aged 55 or older, compared to about 7 percent of the online population.
Four categories of barriers to Internet adoption were identified: incentives, low incomes and affordability, user capability, and infrastructure.
Infrastructure barriers include lack of mobile network coverage, which affected between 1.1 billion and 2.8 billion individuals.

The Internet Barriers Index was created to rank 25 developed and developing countries based on four barrier categories and was found to explain more than half the variance in Internet penetration across countries.
Country profiles examined in depth included China, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Nigeria, and the United States.
The report was conducted in collaboration with Facebook on behalf of Internet.org.
market_data_points: Global online population was approximately 2.7 billion in 2013, with 1.8 billion joining since 2004.
The worldwide Internet user CAGR slowed from 15.1 percent in 2005–2008 to 10.4 percent in 2009–2013.
500 million to 900 million additional people were forecast to join the online population by 2017.
Between 3.8 billion and 4.2 billion people—more than half of the forecasted global population—were projected to remain offline in 2017.
Cisco forecast the online population would reach 3.6 billion users by 2017; Forrester estimated 3.5 billion; Microsoft estimated 4.7 billion by 2025.
3.4 billion of the 4.4 billion offline population lived in just 20 countries.
920 million of the 3.4 billion offline individuals in the top 20 countries were illiterate.
trend_signals: Expansion of mobile network coverage and increasing mobile Internet adoption as a driver of online population growth.
Urbanization as a driver of Internet adoption growth over the past decade.
Shrinking device and data plan prices as a driver of Internet adoption.
Growing middle class as a driver of Internet adoption.
Increasing utility of the Internet as a driver of adoption.
Rate of growth of Internet users is slowing and will continue to slow without significant changes in technology, income growth, economics of access, or policy.
The demographic profile of the offline population (rural, low-income, elderly, illiterate, female) makes it unlikely these individuals will come online solely from trends that drove past adoption.
Lack of relevant local or localized content and services as a persistent barrier to adoption in developing markets.
Lack of trusted logistics and payment systems limiting Internet use cases such as e-commerce and online banking in offline populations.
regulatory_mentions: Limited Internet freedom and information security identified as a root cause of incentive barriers to Internet adoption.
Low ease of doing business in specific regions identified as impeding development of local or localized content and services.
Policies to spur Internet adoption cited as a lever that could change the trajectory of Internet user growth.

sources.title: The next big arenas of competition
key_facts: McKinsey Global Institute identified 18 potential arenas of the future that could reshape the global economy by 2040.
Space is explicitly listed as one of the 18 future arenas of competition identified by McKinsey.
Arenas are defined by two characteristics: high growth and high dynamism, capturing an outsize share of economy's growth with significant market share changes among players.
In 2005, arenas generated only 9 percent of total global economic profit; by 2019 they accounted for 49-50 percent of all economic profit in the biggest companies.

Three combined ingredients in an 'arena-creation potion' tend to generate escalatory competition: business model or technological step changes, escalatory investments, and a large and/or growing addressable market.
In 2020, 33 percent of arenas' total market capitalization was held by companies that had been 'outsiders' in 2005, indicating strong new entrant opportunity in arenas.
In comparison, businesses new to non-arena industries held just 15 percent of total market capitalization, versus 33 percent for arenas.
Sixty-two percent of US business R&D spend went to arenas and arena-adjacent industries in 2005, increasing to 65 percent by 2020.
Arenas spawned a disproportionate number of global giants and offer unusually strong opportunities for new entrants to become powerhouses.
The 12 arenas of today had a revenue compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 10 percent and market capitalization CAGR of 16 percent from 2005 to 2020.
Non-arenas had only a 4 percent revenue CAGR and a 6 percent market cap CAGR over the 2005-2020 period.
market_data_points: 18 future arenas could generate $29 trillion to $48 trillion in revenues by 2040.
18 future arenas could generate $2 trillion to $6 trillion in profit by 2040.
Future arenas' collective share of global GDP could increase from 4 percent to 10 to 16 percent by 2040.
12 arenas of today tripled their global GDP share from 3 to 9 percent between 2005 and 2020.
In 2005, arenas generated $55 billion, or 9 percent of total global economic profit.
By 2019, arenas were generating $250 billion, representing half of total global economic profit.
Arenas had a revenue CAGR of 10 percent and market capitalization CAGR of 16 percent from 2005 to 2020.
Non-arenas had only a 4 percent revenue CAGR and a 6 percent market cap CAGR from 2005 to 2020.
In 2020, 33 percent of arenas' total market capitalization was held by companies that had been outsiders in 2005.
US business R&D spend on arenas and arena-adjacent industries rose from 62 percent in 2005 to 65 percent in 2020.
trend_signals: Space is identified as one of 18 future arenas expected to reshape the global economy by 2040.
Arenas are expected to increase their collective share of global GDP from 4 percent to 10-16 percent by 2040.
New entrants have historically captured disproportionate market share in arenas, suggesting continued disruption potential in emerging industries like space.
Technological step changes and escalatory investment are identified as key precursors to arena formation, both of which are present in satellite communications.
The report signals that industries with large and/or growing addressable markets combined with business model innovation are most likely to become future arenas.
Arenas attract outsize levels of R&D investment, with semiconductors and electrical components accounting for the largest share of US business R&D in arenas.
competitive_mentions: Space is listed as a distinct future arena alongside AI, cloud services, semiconductors, electric vehicles, robotics, and cybersecurity.
Semiconductors are identified as one of the 12 arenas of today with the largest market cap shuffle rate, indicating intense competitive dynamism.
Consumer electronics is identified as one of the 12 arenas of today, relevant to Samsung's existing competitive positioning.
Cloud services, e-commerce, and software are among the top arenas by 2020 market capitalization.
Electric vehicles are identified as both an arena of today and among the 18 future arenas, indicating continued competitive escalation.

sources.title: LEO Satellites: Unlocking Connectivity & Opportunity | BCG
Next-gen satellite internet is transforming pricing, capacity, ...
key_facts: LEO satellite constellations are expected to generate around US$15 billion in annual revenues in 2026.
Deloitte predicts global LEO satellite subscribers will surpass 15 million by end of 2026.
The number of communications satellites in LEO will expand to five constellations made up of over 15,000 to 18,000 satellites by end of 2026.
Spending on direct-to-device (D2D) satellite capacity is predicted to be US$6 to US$8 billion in 2026, with over 1,000 D2D-capable satellites in orbit by year-end.
At end of 2024, an estimated 350 million people (4% of the global population) lived in largely remote areas without mobile internet networks.
LEO ground station terminals cost US$200 to US$500 each, representing a significant affordability barrier in the developing world.
Monthly LEO subscription costs are approximately US$15 at the low end.
D2D actual spending reached around US$4 billion in 2024, surpassing Deloitte's earlier prediction of US$3 billion.
Approximately 85% to 90% of D2D capital spending in 2026 is expected to fund new satellite deployments, with 10% to 15% dedicated to replacing existing satellites.

In low-income, sparsely populated areas, revenues for terrestrial cell networks are about 10 times lower per base station while incurring two to three times higher capital and operating costs than in cities.
By end of 2023, there were around 7,473 active broadband-capable LEO satellites, exceeding Deloitte's earlier forecast of 5,000.
Global satellite data traffic is projected to increase 20 times by end of 2025.
Practical constraints limit sustainable LEO operations to roughly 100,000 active satellites, far below the theoretical maximum of 10–12 million.
LEO broadband has primarily targeted users lacking terrestrial connectivity, but at prices usually higher than equivalent terrestrial broadband services.
In September 2025, one major LEO player purchased blocks of 5G spectrum for direct-to-device connectivity.
By 2028, smartphone users may be able to stream video directly from space to their phones via D2D satellite services.
market_data_points: LEO constellations expected to generate ~US$15 billion in annual revenues in 2026.
Global LEO subscribers predicted to surpass 15 million by end of 2026.
15,000 to 18,000 LEO satellites expected across five constellations by end of 2026.
D2D satellite capacity spending forecast at US$6–8 billion in 2026.
Over 1,000 D2D-capable satellites expected in orbit by end of 2026.
350 million people (4% of global population) lacked mobile internet at end of 2024.
D2D actual spending reached ~US$4 billion in 2024 vs. a predicted ~US$3 billion.
More than 200 million satellite-capable phones were anticipated to be sold in 2024, with nearly US$2 billion in specialty chips.
7,473 active broadband-capable LEO satellites were in orbit by end of 2023.
Average broadband prices in selected developed markets range from US$33 to US$80 per month.
Some developing markets have broadband prices under US$10 per month.
Developing markets such as Brazil and South Africa have broadband prices in the US$21 to US$48 per month range.
LEO ground station terminals cost US$200 to US$500 each.
Global satellite data traffic expected to increase 20 times by end of 2025.
Theoretical LEO capacity could support 10–12 million satellites; practical limit is ~100,000 active satellites.
trend_signals: Direct-to-device (D2D) satellite connectivity is proliferating but faces unresolved monetization and business model challenges.
New LEO constellations are entering the market in 2026 and beyond, increasing competition.
Amazon Kuiper plans to enter LEO broadband market in 2026 with a low-cost monthly pricing model targeting underserved developing regions.
China is building two LEO mega constellations: Guowang and Qianfan (G60/Spacesail).
The European IRIS² and Canada's Telesat Lightspeed are planned LEO constellations approaching deployment.
Regional initiatives such as UAE-based Orbitworks are emerging in satellite connectivity.
Eutelsat OneWeb is upgrading its constellation to expand capacity, improve latency, and enable D2D connectivity.
Two distinct distribution strategies are emerging: cooperation with local telcos and direct competition with terrestrial providers.
LEO providers are beginning to compete directly with terrestrial telcos in developing markets through more affordable subscription models.
Some portion of LEO subscriber growth has come at the expense of geostationary equatorial orbit (GEO) internet providers.
New satellite capacity technologies are needed for LEO to support densely populated areas beyond a few dozen simultaneous users.
By 2028, smartphone video streaming directly from space via D2D is anticipated.
Global regulators and standards bodies are rapidly accommodating non-terrestrial networks by allocating spectrum and finalizing 5G NTN specifications.
competitive_mentions: Starlink: Dominant LEO broadband provider; noted to face spectrum constraints despite global reach.
Amazon Kuiper: Planning market entry in 2026 with low-cost pricing model targeting developing markets.
China Guowang: Broadband mega constellation in development, placing satellites in orbit in 2026 or coming years.
Qianfan (G60/Spacesail): Chinese LEO constellation project in development.
Telesat Lightspeed (Canada): LEO constellation planned for deployment.
European IRIS²: EU LEO constellation planned for deployment.
Eutelsat OneWeb (Europe): Established operator upgrading constellation for capacity, latency, and D2D.
Orbitworks (UAE): Regional LEO satellite venture emerging from the United Arab Emirates.
Geostationary equatorial orbit (GEO) internet providers: Losing market share to LEO competitors.
regulatory_mentions: Global regulators and industry standards bodies have moved to allocate spectrum and finalize 5G non-terrestrial network (NTN) specifications to allow ordinary phones to connect seamlessly to satellites.
Regulatory requirements related to spectrum availability in Ku-band and Ka-band frequency bands can limit satellite providers' ability to expand capacity.
Regulatory delays, alongside collision risks and tracking inaccuracies, limit sustainable LEO operations to roughly 100,000 active satellites.
Spectrum management is emerging as a pivotal regulatory factor for sustainable satellite growth and integration with terrestrial networks.
One major LEO player purchased blocks of 5G spectrum in September 2025 to enable direct-to-device connectivity.

sources.title: The Impact of Satellite Constellations and LEO Technology
key_facts: Satellite constellations led by Starlink are turning satellite connectivity into a mainstream solution through massive investments ranging from USD 10 to 30 billion.
LEO constellation satellite costs have been dropping at approximately 15% per year since 2021.
Starlink has over 4 million subscribers as of 2024, significantly outpacing competitors.
Starlink operates a constellation of more than 4,500 satellites enabling home broadband, maritime, and in-flight connectivity.
In Kenya, constellation pricing is directly competitive with local telecom operators, and superior speeds are making them an increasingly attractive choice for consumers.
Starlink's V2 Mini satellites are already equipped with direct-to-cell functionality, enabling smartphones to connect without hardware modifications.
Direct-to-cell technology allows satellites to connect directly with standard mobile phones, providing seamless coverage without terrestrial network infrastructure.
eSIM technology enables satellite operators to directly connect with customers, bypassing traditional mobile telcos by eliminating the need for local SIM distribution and carrier partnerships.

Direct-to-cell technology relies on L, S, and 600–900 MHz frequency bands, which are already allocated to terrestrial operators, requiring satellite providers to negotiate agreements with local telecom players.
In Europe, where the market remains highly fragmented, at least one operator in each country is likely to be open to leasing its frequencies for satellite use.
Starlink's total spending on its constellation now exceeds the total investment of the traditional satellite sector.

Satellite operators including AST SpaceMobile, Lynk, and Starlink have already demonstrated direct-to-cell feasibility with 4G connectivity established from space without requiring hardware modifications on mobile devices.
eSIM platforms such as Airalo, Nomad, and Holafly could enable constellations to directly address customers as connectivity providers in underserved areas, bypassing traditional operators.

Telecom operators face three strategic options in response to satellite market entry: resisting entry via regulatory influence, partnering with constellations for B2C distribution, or developing their own competing solutions.
market_data_points: Satellite capacity is set to double annually until 2028, far outpacing the 19% growth of older geostationary models.
Satellite connectivity costs have declined approximately 15% per year since 2021.
Starlink has over 4 million subscribers as of 2024.
Starlink operates more than 4,500 satellites as of the time of publication.
Investments in leading satellite constellations range from USD 10 to 30 billion.
Declining satellite connectivity prices are expected to continue well beyond 2035.
In the U.S., approximately 4 million customers in rural areas lacking fiber access now rely on satellite broadband.
trend_signals: Non-GEO (LEO and MEO) satellite capacity is forecast to double annually through 2028, far exceeding geostationary satellite growth of 19%.
Connectivity prices are expected to continue declining well beyond 2035 as multiple LEO operators scale their networks.
Direct-to-cell satellite technology is emerging as the next frontier, enabling standard smartphones to connect via satellite without hardware changes.
eSIM adoption is expected to enable satellite operators to bypass traditional telco distribution channels and connect directly with end users.
Satellite constellations are transitioning from a niche, business-focused industry toward a mass-market consumer offering.
Spectrum collaboration between satellite operators and local telcos is expected to become increasingly critical as satellite networks expand into mobile markets.
Regulatory bodies in Europe are viewed as likely facilitators of satellite-terrestrial spectrum agreements to bridge rural connectivity gaps.
The lines between traditional telecom and satellite operators are blurring due to the rise of non-GEO satellites and new technologies.
Satellite broadband is moving into direct competition with traditional telecom providers in home broadband, competing on both pricing and performance.
competitive_mentions: Starlink (SpaceX): Market leader with 4 million+ subscribers, 4,500+ satellites, and V2 Mini direct-to-cell capability; spending exceeds total traditional satellite sector investment.
Amazon Kuiper: Named as a major planned large-scale constellation rollout player.
OneWeb: Named as a major planned large-scale constellation rollout player.
Telesat: Named as a major planned large-scale constellation rollout player.
SES: Named as a legacy satellite operator whose investment is dwarfed by new constellation entrants like Starlink.
AST SpaceMobile: Has demonstrated direct-to-cell 4G connectivity from space.
Lynk: Has demonstrated direct-to-cell 4G connectivity from space.
Airalo, Nomad, Holafly: eSIM platforms that could be leveraged by satellite constellations to reach end customers directly, bypassing traditional operators.
regulatory_mentions: Direct-to-cell satellite technology relies on L, S, and 600–900 MHz frequency bands already allocated to terrestrial operators, requiring negotiated agreements with local telecoms for spectrum access.

Regulators in Europe could play a key role in facilitating spectrum-sharing agreements between satellite operators and local telecoms, viewing satellite solutions as a tool to bridge rural connectivity gaps.
Telecom operators can attempt to resist satellite constellation market entry by influencing regulatory bodies, though this is noted as not a long-term solution.

sources.title: Navigating space - KPMG agentic corporate services
key_facts: KPMG International and the Space Foundation interviewed nearly two dozen industry and defense leaders at the highest levels of the space domain for this report.
Ground stations were attacked during the 1991 Gulf War and in the 2011 conflict in Libya, demonstrating the vulnerability of space assets in conflict.
The jamming of SatCom and GPS networks has been reported in numerous regions and theaters of conflict.
Countries including Australia, Canada, China, France, India, Japan, Russia, the UK, and the US are establishing space commands to develop domestic capabilities and enable foreign partnerships.
African countries placed 41 satellites into orbit in 2019 alone.
Middle Eastern nations have national strategic priorities in the space domain, including the launch of Mars-bound missions.
Governments and commercial players are moving away from large 'exquisite' satellite configurations toward diversified constellations to create additional redundancy and resilience in networks.
Satellites and spacecraft are described as inherently vulnerable to cyber-attacks, jamming/spoofing, and physical attacks.
Commercial ventures are increasingly offering Earth Observation data in near real-time as off-the-shelf solutions.
Space sustainability and debris management are increasingly being viewed as national security issues as markets and societies become more dependent on space assets.
Gen. John W. Raymond, Chief of Space Operations, US Space Force, stated that space will become the most vital domain for national security, surpassing air, land, and sea.
The report was produced in partnership with KPMG Lower Gulf Limited, licensed in the United Arab Emirates.
market_data_points: Between 2019 and 2020, the number of spacecraft launched per year more than doubled.
Expectations indicate there will likely be 100,000 satellites in orbit by the end of the decade (from a 2021 baseline).
African countries placed 41 satellites into orbit in 2019 alone.
It took almost 70 years for the air force to be fully integrated into most joint forces; most interviewees expect the integration of the space domain to be much faster.
trend_signals: Space is predicted to become the dominant domain for national security by 2030.
Barriers to entry into the space domain are falling, enabling a growing number of governmental and commercial players.
The pace of innovation in space is predicted to continue to quicken, with new capabilities emerging and scaling rapidly.
Open Source Intelligence from commercial Earth Observation data is expected to rival classified sources within the next few years.
Geointelligence singularity from Earth Observation is expected to be enabled through AI and mobile technologies.
Cislunar space is expected to become increasingly interesting and regularly populated, with the foundations of real space logistics emerging.
Space manufacturing and proximity operations (e.g., refueling vehicles) are identified as breakthrough innovation areas.
Commercial companies are increasingly offering satellite communication and Earth observation capabilities as off-the-shelf solutions, reducing reliance on government-developed systems.
Space sustainability is forecast to become a top national security issue as debris and traffic density increase in low earth orbit.
Cyber security and resilience capabilities in the space domain are expected to evolve rapidly.
competitive_mentions: SpaceX is cited as a leading non-governmental commercial venture crowding into the space domain.
HawkEye 360 is mentioned as a commercial player with a model centered on higher quantities of lower-cost satellites on faster timelines.
The Aerospace Corporation is referenced in the context of AI and geointelligence capabilities.
Lockheed Martin Space is cited in the context of space sustainability and debris concerns.
The US Space Force is noted as perhaps the most public defense organization realigning to recognize the importance of space.
The historical US-Soviet 'space race' is cited as the origin of competition in the space domain.
regulatory_mentions: Achieving broad consensus around global norms of behavior and policy is described as critical to humanity's ability to benefit from the space domain.
International law is cited as needing to come together around space sustainability and debris concerns.
The need to define 'rules of the road' for the space domain is identified as urgent given the growing number of space-faring nations and companies.
The Outer Space Treaty and broader international legal frameworks are implicitly referenced in the context of alignment on norms unlocking advancement.

sources.title: Communications Review - Going further
key_facts: PwC's Communications Industry practice delivers assurance, tax and advisory services to telecom, cable, satellite and Internet service providers across the globe.

Emerging economies are increasingly adopting Internet-enabled devices, increasing data demand and creating an environment that shares many characteristics seen in the US and Western Europe three to five years ago.
Mobile operators can fuel greater revenues with increased data usage in emerging markets by viewing digital markets as inter-reliant networks.
Augmenting the capacity and coverage of mobile networks with small cells is rapidly becoming accepted as a high-priority solution throughout the telecom industry.
Revenue assurance is gaining renewed attention within many operators as products and services become more complex, markets mature and margin pressure increases.
Telcos are spending significant amounts on new infrastructure but the process of allocating and managing capital is described as both deeply flawed and deeply frustrating.
A small but growing number of operators are attempting to optimize capital expenditure as markets mature and quick wins on operating expenditure dry up.
market_data_points: Emerging economies' digital market environment is described as sharing many characteristics seen in the US and Western Europe three to five years prior to the publication date.
trend_signals: Small cells are rapidly becoming a high-priority solution for augmenting mobile network capacity and coverage.
Emerging markets are experiencing accelerating adoption of Internet-enabled devices driving data demand growth.
The telecom industry is moving towards a data-driven future requiring realignment of revenue assurance functions.
Mobile operators in emerging markets are positioned to find new revenue opportunities through increased data usage.
Operators are increasingly focused on cracking the 'capex code' as markets mature and operating expenditure savings diminish.
Industry convergence is a major challenge being addressed by telecom operators globally.
competitive_mentions: Verizon Communications is cited as one of the few US telecom operators to come out on top amid regulation, innovation, consolidation, competition and technology changes.
Equipment vendors and network operators are still searching for profitable business models for small cell transformation.
regulatory_mentions: PwC anticipates and helps clients deal with the impact of global regulatory change in the telecom industry.
Regulation is cited alongside innovation, consolidation, competition and technology as forces that have reshaped the US telecoms industry.

sources.title: Satellite cybersecurity: Safeguarding the final frontier
Regional trends in global sourcing
key_facts: The PBEC-KPMG-Monash University report analyzes a sample of 132 companies that are considering or have already altered their supply chain sourcing, covering 232 market relocations between 2018 and 2023.
Most of the capacity movements are in Asia, broken down as follows: 16% in North Asia, 55% in Southeast Asia, 12% in Europe, and 17% in the Americas.
Vietnam tops the list with 70 companies that relocated or diverted production there, followed by Taiwan (24), Thailand (20), and India (18).
Many capacity moves were to multiple markets (44%), highlighting the increased complexity of observed sourcing patterns and the further fragmentation of global supply chains.
The dominant company headquarters among the 132 companies are the U.S. (34%), Taiwan (24%), Japan (21%), and China, including Hong Kong SAR (14%).
More than 75% of the 132 companies analyzed are valued at over USD 1 billion in market capitalization.
Southeast Asia still dominates the sourcing move away from China.
Companies are adjusting supply chain and inventory management policies, including shifts from 'Just-In-Time' to 'Just-In-Case', near-shoring and on-shoring, and the emergence of micro supply chains.
Supply-side risks regarding access to sustainable materials and general raw materials are among the highest-ranked concerns among business leaders.
Transportation costs, delivery reliability, supplier capacity, and the financial stability of suppliers are still key concerns in moving capacity or entering a new market for the first time.
Much of the relocated distribution has remained in Asia (71%), with 55% centered in Southeast Asia.
Taiwan, Thailand, India, and Mexico have predominantly received sourcing moves in electronics.
The data was collected through web scraping of 1,089 relevant news articles from multiple sources published between 1 January 2016 and 31 January 2022.
market_data_points: The latest IMF forecasts predict EMDE (Emerging Market and Developing Economies) Asia will grow 20% faster than the global average in the year of publication.
Vietnam received 70 sourcing relocation moves, Taiwan 24, Thailand 20, India 18, USA 19, Mexico 19, Indonesia 12, Cambodia 10, Japan 9, Malaysia 9, and the Philippines 7.
55% of company capacity relocations between 2018 and 2023 were centered in Southeast Asia.
44% of capacity moves were to multiple markets.
132 companies analyzed covering 232 market relocations between 2018 and 2023.
1,089 news articles were collected from sources published between 1 January 2016 and 31 January 2022.
13% of the 132 companies are valued at $100 billion or more; 27% are valued between $1 billion and $5 billion.
In 2018, 11 companies announced sourcing changes; 36 in 2019; 32 in 2020; 18 in 2021; 31 in 2022; and 4 planned for 2023.
trend_signals: Shift from 'Just-In-Time' to 'Just-In-Case' inventory management is an emerging trend among Asia Pacific companies.
Near-shoring and on-shoring are emerging as supply chain strategies among multinational companies.
Micro supply chains are emerging as an alternative to traditional global supply chain structures.
India shows the greatest potential for future sourcing patterns to emerge among Asia Pacific markets.
Increasing appetite for investments in technology to enable increased visibility and traceability to manage supply chains.
Companies are upgrading IT capabilities and cybersecurity protocols and announcing strategic partnerships in the ESG specialist space.
The global business community is placing increasing importance on the development of a digitally-enabled circular economy.
Asia Pacific business leaders hold a more bullish view on globalisation compared to global peers.
Companies involved in electronics, automotive, and footwear were early movers in adjusting sourcing locations, followed by clothing, household, and component industries from 2020 onwards.
competitive_mentions: U.S.-China trade tensions are a primary driver of supply chain relocation decisions among multinational companies.
The Trump administration's 'America First' policy (2018-2019) created impetus for companies to return production to the U.S.
China's mature manufacturing infrastructure means that more than one alternative sourcing destination is needed to meet demands of capacity moves away from China.
Mexico is the biggest sourcing relocation beneficiary outside of Asia for companies seeking proximity to the U.S. market, with 19 sourcing moves recorded.
regulatory_mentions: Economic sanctions imposed on Russia are identified as a factor influencing global sourcing and supply chain decisions.
The increasing politicisation of economic trade and its encompassment through the lens of national security policy is identified as a key trend affecting sourcing decisions.
Governments in the Asia Pacific region continue to support new economic expansion with various measures, tax incentives, and schemes to attract manufacturers, suppliers, founders, and investors.
U.S.-China trade tensions and related tariff policies are cited as a major driver of supply chain relocation decisions.

sources.title: 2025 Digital Media Trends: Social platforms are becoming ...
key_facts: Social video platforms now draw over half of US ad spending.
49% of consumers surveyed currently have a cable or satellite TV subscription, down from 63% three years ago.
The primary reasons subscribers pay for cable or satellite TV are to watch live news (43%) and sports (41%).
23% of Generation Z and 18% of millennial cable subscribers intend to terminate their subscriptions within the next 12 months, compared to only 8% of boomers.
Subscribers report spending an average of $125 per month on cable or satellite TV subscriptions.
Subscribers report spending an average of $69 per month for four paid streaming services combined.
Live-streaming TV subscribers report spending 35% less monthly on average than cable or satellite subscribers.
Live-streaming TV subscription growth has stagnated at around 40% of households for the past two years.
53% of consumers surveyed say their SVOD subscriptions are the paid media and entertainment services they use most frequently.
41% of consumers overall say the content available on SVOD isn't worth the price, up five percentage points from the 2024 report.
Roughly half (47%) of consumers say they pay too much for the streaming services they use.
The average number of paid SVOD services has remained at four per subscribing household.
The overall cost subscribers pay for SVOD has gone up 13% in the past year, from an average of $61 per month to $69.
Gen Z and millennials, with an average of 5 paid SVOD services, have seen a 20% increase in costs.
The average price for a premium, ad-free SVOD service subscription is around $16 per month.
Consumers surveyed say $14 is 'just the right price' for an ad-free subscription to their favorite SVOD service, with $25 being deemed too expensive.
A price hike of $5 would make 60% of respondents likely to cancel their favorite SVOD service.
About half of US households say they have no money left over at the end of the month after meeting their expenses, according to Deloitte's January 2025 ConsumerSignals survey.
The median household annual income in the United States is about US$80,000.
Global ad revenues for TV, including streaming video, are expected to see slow growth of around 2.4% in coming years.
US consumers spend an average of six hours of daily media and entertainment time per person.
A third of Gen Z respondents say they don't subscribe to an SVOD service to watch sports because they watch clips and highlights on social media.
43% of Gen Z and millennials surveyed indicate a willingness to pay more for streaming video subscriptions that include access to live sports.
27% of consumers said live sports is the type of content they spend the most time watching on SVOD.
market_data_points: Cable or satellite TV subscription penetration fell from 63% to 49% over three years (as of 2025 survey).
Average monthly cable/satellite TV spend: $125 per subscriber.
Average monthly spend on four paid SVOD services: $69 per subscribing household.
SVOD monthly cost increased 13% year-over-year, from $61 to $69 per household.
Gen Z and millennial SVOD costs rose 20% year-over-year to an average of 5 paid services.
Live-streaming TV penetration stagnant at ~40% of households for two years.
Global TV ad revenue (including streaming) forecast growth of ~2.4% annually.
Social video platforms account for over half of US ad spending.
Average 'acceptable' price for favorite ad-free SVOD service: $14/month; $25 deemed too expensive.
Current average premium ad-free SVOD price: ~$16/month.
60% of subscribers would likely cancel their favorite SVOD service given a $5 price increase.
Deloitte January 2025 ConsumerSignals: ~50% of US households have no money left over after monthly expenses.
trend_signals: Social video platforms are becoming the dominant force in media and entertainment, displacing traditional studios and SVOD services for both audience time and advertiser dollars.
Pay TV (cable and satellite) subscriptions are in long-term structural decline, particularly among younger generations.
Younger generations (Gen Z, millennials) are shifting entertainment consumption toward social video, SVOD, gaming, and audio rather than linear TV.
Consumer subscription fatigue is growing, with frustration over rising prices and managing multiple subscriptions.
SVOD services are approaching a critical price threshold beyond which subscriber churn accelerates significantly.
Live sports and live news remain the key retention drivers for traditional pay TV.
Social media platforms are cannibalizing sports viewership by offering free clips and highlights, reducing the perceived need for pay TV or SVOD sports packages.

key_facts: The Satellites Market is projected to grow from USD 15.68 billion in 2025 to USD 46.79 billion by 2031, with a CAGR of 16.9%.

Asia Pacific accounted for a 39.3% revenue share in the satellites market in 2025.
Asia Pacific is expected to be the fastest-growing satellite market during the forecast period, driven by expanding national space programs and rising satellite launches.
Communication satellites are expected to be the largest application segment during the forecast period due to high demand for broadband connectivity, broadcasting, and secure data links.
The small satellites segment is expected to register the highest CAGR of 23.8% during the forecast period.
The commercial segment is expected to hold the largest market share, supported by increased investments from private satellite operators and service providers.
The Ku-band is expected to dominate the frequency segment due to its widespread use in satellite communication services.
Large-scale LEO constellation deployments are cutting deployment time and lowering satellite costs through standardized manufacturing and rideshare launches.
Spectrum allocation and slow licensing processes in many countries are delaying satellite network rollouts, increasing time to market.
SpaceX, Thales Alenia Space, and Lockheed Martin Corporation were identified as the star players in the satellites market.
SpaceX leads with a large-scale LEO constellation and vertically integrated satellite manufacturing and launch capabilities.
The market size in 2024 was USD 14.17 billion.
Higher satellite density in crowded LEO orbits leads to more close approach events and raises regulatory concerns about long-term sustainability.
Satellite operators are increasingly shifting toward data-as-a-service models, monetizing processed insights rather than raw capacity.
In May 2025, CNH Industrial entered a partnership with Starlink to integrate satellite-based broadband connectivity across its agricultural equipment portfolio.
In December 2025, the US Space Force confirmed deployment of the MILNET satellite communications constellation with SpaceX, comprising approximately 480 LEO small satellites.
Countries including China, India, Japan, and South Korea are driving higher investment in defense and civil space missions in the Asia Pacific region.
Regulatory uncertainty around ITU filings, local approvals, and coordination with terrestrial networks can delay constellation expansion plans and limit service availability in key regions.

sources.title: Communication Small Satellite Market Size, Share & ...
key_facts: The Communication Small Satellite Market is projected to grow from USD 5.95 billion in 2025 to USD 18.34 billion by 2030 at a CAGR of 25.2%.
In terms of volume, the communication small satellite market is expected to grow from 3,028 units in 2025 to 4,396 units by 2030.
The Communication Small Satellite Market was valued at USD 3.53 billion in 2024.
The North American communication small satellite market accounted for a 54.1% share in 2025.
The commercial segment is projected to register the highest CAGR of 25.7% in the communication small satellite market.

The LEO segment is projected to dominate the communication small satellite market in 2025, driven by the rising deployment of dense communication constellations aimed at achieving global, low-latency coverage.
The Ku-band (12 to 18 GHz) segment is expected to capture the largest market share owing to increasing adoption for mobility, enterprise connectivity, and high-throughput links.
The mini satellite (101-1,200 KG) segment is projected to dominate the market by mass.
The satellite bus segment is expected to capture the largest market share by system component.
SpaceX leads the communication small satellite market with a strong product portfolio, manufacturing technologies, and a broad customer base.
BAE Systems is recognized as an emerging leader in the communication small satellite market.
North America is projected to register the highest CAGR during the forecast period in the communication small satellite market.
The laser/optical (200–400 THz) segment is projected to grow at the fastest rate from 2025 to 2030 by frequency.

In December 2025, Telesat entered a strategic agreement with the Government of Canada and MDA Space to develop next-generation military satellite communications capabilities under the Enhanced Satellite Communication Project – Polar.
In July 2025, Thales Alenia Space signed a contract with GovSat to build GovSat-2, a defense-oriented geostationary communications satellite operating in X, Ka, and UHF bands.
